A lower component can do uvm_config_db #(T)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env", "name", value), and the parent calls get() afterwards (after the child's build_phase, for example in connect_phase), because set and get are matched at run time. A cleaner way to pass information upward is through a TLM analysis port, a callback, or a shared configuration object handle.
how would you write a test with bounded: Declare the input fields as rand in a transaction class and add constraints for the bounds, for example constraint c_range { addr inside {[0:1023]}; len inside {[1:16]}; }, or use $urandom_range(max, min) in a simple testbench. Bias towards corners with dist (for example more weight on 0 and the maximum value), use inline randomize() with { } for specific tests, check that randomize() returns 1, and add functional coverage to confirm the bounds and corner values were actually hit.
is an lpddr5 phy backward compatible: LPDDR5 itself is not backward compatible with LPDDR4 at the device level: it uses different clocking (a separate WCK data clock), voltages and protocol features. But many LPDDR5 controller and PHY IPs are designed as combo PHYs that support LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X as well (and LPDDR5X), switching modes in configuration. So the answer depends on the specific PHY: check its datasheet for supported standards.
print a binary tree in zig zag order: Do a level-order (breadth-first) traversal with a queue, processing one level at a time, and keep a flag for the direction: collect each level's values in a list and reverse it on every other level before printing. A two-stack version avoids reversing: push children left-then-right for one direction and right-then-left for the other. Time O(n), space O(width of the tree).
what is the difference between always an: An initial block runs once, starting at time 0, and is used in testbenches for stimulus and setup (and on FPGAs for initial register values); synthesis otherwise ignores it. An always block runs repeatedly forever, re-triggered by its sensitivity list or timing controls; always @(posedge clk) describes flip-flops and always @(*) combinational logic, so it is the synthesizable construct for hardware.
write a sequence that sends 10 back to b: Keep the type of the previous command in the sequence and constrain the next one: in body(), loop 10 times; create the item; start_item(); randomize with { if (prev_was_write) cmd != READ; }; finish_item(); then set prev_was_write = (item.cmd == WRITE). The first item is unconstrained (it may be a write). Alternatively randomize an array of 10 commands at once with constraint foreach (c[i]) if (i > 0 && c[i-1] == WRITE) c[i] != READ;.
what array types does systemverilog have: Packed arrays (bit [7:0] a) are a contiguous vector that can be used as a number. Unpacked fixed-size arrays (int a[8]) hold separate elements. Dynamic arrays (int a[]) are sized at run time with new[]. Associative arrays (int a[string] or a[int]) are sparse and indexed by any key, good for memory models. Queues (int q[$]) grow and shrink at both ends with push_back, pop_front and insert. They come with methods such as size, delete, sort, find and sum.
design an inverter using digital logic b: An inverter can be built from a NAND gate with its inputs tied together (or one input tied to 1), from a NOR gate with inputs tied together (or one input tied to 0), from an XOR gate with one input tied to 1, from a 2:1 MUX with d0 = 1, d1 = 0 and the signal on the select, or from a decoder output. The point is that any universal gate can make NOT.
how do you size the transistors of an in: Size the PMOS wider than the NMOS to balance rise and fall delays, because hole mobility is about 2 to 3 times lower than electron mobility: typically Wp/Wn = 2 to 3 for equal drive and a switching threshold near VDD/2. Then scale both up together for the load: a larger inverter drives more capacitance faster but presents more input capacitance to the previous stage, so chains are sized with a constant fan-out of about 4 per stage (logical effort).
what are the characteristics of cmos: Near-zero static power (only leakage, because no DC path exists in steady state), full rail-to-rail output swing, high noise margins, very high input impedance, inverting gates built from complementary pull-up and pull-down networks, delay set by charging load capacitance, and excellent scaling and density. Its main power cost is dynamic switching power, plus leakage in advanced nodes.
why is cmos used to implement logic gate: CMOS gates draw almost no static current, give full logic levels and good noise margins, have very high input impedance so one gate can drive many others, and scale well to billions of transistors on a chip. The complementary networks make logic design regular (series and parallel transistors map to AND and OR), and the process is cheap and mature.
explain pipeline design and pipeline haz: Pipeline design splits a long path into stages separated by registers so that a new operation can start every cycle; throughput rises and the clock gets faster, at the cost of latency and registers. Hazards are cases where the next instruction cannot proceed: structural (resource conflicts), data (dependencies on results not ready yet, fixed by forwarding and stalls) and control (branches, fixed by prediction and flushing). Balancing stage delays and handling hazards are the main design tasks.
explain pipelining: Pipelining breaks a task into stages and overlaps them, like an assembly line: while one item is in stage 3, the next is in stage 2 and the one after in stage 1. Each stage has its own register, so after the pipeline fills one result comes out every clock. It increases throughput and allows a higher clock frequency; latency per item increases slightly, and dependencies between items cause hazards.
how does pipelining increase a design s: The clock period must cover the longest combinational path between registers. Inserting pipeline registers cuts a long path into shorter ones, so the worst stage delay, and therefore the minimum period, gets smaller: ideally a path of delay T split into k balanced stages allows a period of about T/k plus register overhead (clock-to-Q, setup and skew). The overhead limits the gain from very deep pipelines.
what are the stages of a 5 stage pipelin: Instruction Fetch (read the instruction at PC from instruction memory and compute PC + 4), Instruction Decode (decode, read the register file, sign-extend immediates, detect hazards), Execute (ALU operation, address calculation, branch comparison), Memory access (load or store data memory), and Write Back (write the result to the register file).
explain the scan insertion steps: Read the netlist and libraries, define the test protocol (scan clocks, resets, scan enable, test mode), and run DFT design rule checks to find uncontrollable clocks and resets, latches and loops. Then replace flops with scan flops, decide the number and length of chains (balanced, per clock domain and edge), stitch the chains with lockup latches where domains or edges mix, connect scan-in, scan-out and scan-enable ports (possibly with compression logic), re-run DRC, and write out the scan netlist, the scan DEF for chain reordering in placement, and the test protocol for ATPG.
a 100 um wire has 100 us of delay buffer: Wire delay grows with the square of length (distributed RC), so the 100 um wire's 100 us scales as L^2. Segments of 20, 30 and 50 um give 100 x (0.2^2 + 0.3^2 + 0.5^2) = 100 x 0.38 = 38 us of wire delay, plus 2 buffers x 30 us = 60 us, so about 98 us in total: slightly better than 100 us. (Equal segments would do better; with a linear wire model the buffers would only add delay.)
design a circuit that produces a given t: Read the diagram cycle by cycle: list the output value in each clock cycle against the inputs, and decide whether the output depends only on the current inputs (combinational), on past values (flops or counters), or on a sequence (an FSM). Write a state table, choose the state encoding, derive the next-state and output equations with K-maps, and check the result by drawing its waveform against the given one, including the reset behaviour.
design a state machine that outputs 1 fo: Use a Moore or Mealy FSM. Mealy with two states: S0 (last bit was 0 or reset) and S1 (last bit was 1); in S1, an input of 1 outputs 1 and stays in S1 (overlapping, so 111 gives two outputs), and a 0 goes back to S0. Equivalently, register the previous bit and output in & prev. If the pairs must not overlap, go from S1 to S0 after a match instead.
explain packed versus unpacked arrays in: Packed dimensions are declared before the name (bit [7:0][3:0] p) and are stored contiguously as one vector, so the whole array can be used as a number, sliced, and assigned with arithmetic; only bit-level types can be packed. Unpacked dimensions come after the name (int u [4][8]) and are separate elements, which can be of any type, are accessed element by element, and are how memories are modelled. You can mix them: logic [7:0] mem [0:255] is 256 unpacked bytes.
explain the main atpg concepts: ATPG automatically generates test patterns for a fault model, usually stuck-at and transition faults on a scan design. For each fault it activates the fault (sets the faulty node to the opposite value), propagates the effect to a scan flop or output, and justifies the required values back to controllable inputs (D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN). Fault simulation then drops all other faults the pattern detects, and pattern compaction merges patterns. Results are reported as fault coverage and test coverage; untestable and redundant faults are classified separately.
find patterns that detect given faults: For each fault, first activate it: set the faulty line to the opposite of its stuck value. Then sensitise a path to an output: set every side input of gates along the path to its non-controlling value (1 for AND and NAND, 0 for OR and NOR). Finally justify all those values back to the primary inputs. Write the resulting input vector and verify that the good and faulty circuits give different outputs; one vector often detects several faults.
find the error in a mux based programmab: A programmable delay line built from a chain of delay cells with multiplexers that select a tap. Typical errors: glitches when the select changes while the signal is high (change the select only when the input is stable, or resynchronise it), unequal mux delays making the steps non-monotonic, an inverted or reversed select ordering, missing buffering between taps, and not accounting for PVT variation of the delay cells. Check monotonicity and glitch-free switching.
given a pulse detector circuit identify: A pulse detector usually samples a signal with flops and compares current and delayed values. It fails when the pulse is shorter than a clock period (it can fall between two edges and be missed), when the input is asynchronous and not synchronised (metastability), when two pulses come closer than the detector's recovery time, at reset or power-up when the delayed copy is X, and when glitches create false detections. The fix is to synchronise, stretch short pulses or use a toggle-based crossing.
given two waveforms design logic that ge: Compare the waveforms cycle by cycle and find the relationship: a delay (flops), a frequency division (a counter or toggle flop), an edge-triggered pulse (a flop and an AND or XOR with the delayed copy), a duty-cycle change (counting on both edges), or a combination. Then build the minimum logic and check that the reset value and the phase relative to the clock match.
how does a given rc network behave at di: Treat capacitors as open at low frequency and as short at high frequency (inductors the reverse), then see which path dominates. For an RC network that means finding whether the output is taken across C (low-pass: passes DC, rolls off above 1/(2 pi R C)) or across R (high-pass: blocks DC, passes high frequencies). Around the corner frequency the gain is -3 dB and the phase 45 degrees; beyond it, the gain falls at 20 dB per decade per pole.
what is the difference between reg and w: A wire is a net: it has no storage and must be continuously driven, by an assign statement or a module output. A reg is a variable that holds the last value assigned to it in an always or initial block. Despite its name, a reg does not have to be a register: in always @(*) it becomes combinational logic. SystemVerilog replaces both in most code with logic, which can be driven either way (by a single driver).
what optimizations should you use when w: Maximise parallelism and memory efficiency: enough threads to fill the GPU (occupancy), coalesced global memory accesses so a warp reads contiguous addresses, tiling to reuse data in shared memory or registers, avoiding shared-memory bank conflicts, minimising branch divergence within a warp, using tensor cores and lower precision where possible, overlapping data transfers with compute, fusing kernels to reduce memory round-trips, and checking with a profiler whether the kernel is memory- or compute-bound.
write a script that retimes registers: Retiming moves registers across combinational logic to balance stage delays without changing behaviour. A script would read the netlist and timing report, find stages whose slack is unbalanced, and move registers backward across a gate (one register on each input replaced by one on the output) or forward, keeping the number of registers on every cycle in the circuit the same; then rerun timing. In practice you enable the synthesis tool's retiming option and use the script to choose which modules or paths it may touch.
write multiplication code in assembly: Without a multiply instruction, use shift and add: clear the result; loop while the multiplier is not zero: if its lowest bit is 1, add the multiplicand to the result; shift the multiplicand left and the multiplier right. With a multiply instruction it is one line (MUL r3, r1, r2 on Arm or RISC-V). Mention overflow (the product needs twice the width) and the signed case.
why are fuses important in an soc: Fuses (eFuses or anti-fuses) are one-time-programmable bits blown at test time or in the field. They store chip-specific data that must survive power-off: memory repair information (which redundant rows or columns replace failing ones), trimming values for analog blocks and PLLs, unique IDs and calibration, secure boot keys and security settings, and feature or SKU configuration. They are read by a fuse controller at boot.
explain the main features of the apb and: APB is the simple, low-power peripheral bus: no pipelining, a two-phase transfer (setup with PSEL, then access with PENABLE), an optional PREADY for wait states and PSLVERR for errors, used for register access. AHB is a higher-performance bus: pipelined address and data phases, bursts (incrementing and wrapping), wider data, a single master per transfer with arbitration in multi-master systems, HREADY for wait states and HRESP for errors. AXI goes further with separate channels and outstanding transactions.
find the maximum element in a rotated sh: Use a modified binary search for the rotation point: compare a[mid] with a[hi]; if a[mid] > a[hi], the drop (and the maximum just before it) is in the right half, otherwise in the left. The maximum is the element just before the minimum (or the last element if the array is not rotated). This is O(log n); with duplicates it can degrade to O(n).
for a given circuit calculate the maximu: Find the longest register-to-register path. fmax = 1 / (Tclk-to-Q + Tcomb,max + Tsetup + Tskew_effect + uncertainty), where a capture clock that arrives later than the launch clock helps setup. Also check hold separately (Tclk-to-Q + Tcomb,min >= Thold + skew), because hold does not depend on frequency.
why does pcie 6 0 use a larger header: PCIe 6.0 moved to PAM4 signalling with FLIT (flow control unit) mode, adding forward error correction and a stronger CRC, and it extended the TLP header format to carry more information (for example additional fields and prefixes for new features). These additions improve reliability at 64 GT/s and support new capabilities, at the cost of a few more header and protection bytes per transfer.
what is the difference between a task an: A function executes in zero time and cannot block, returns a value (or is void), and can be called from expressions and constraints; it may only call functions. A task can block and consume time (delays, waits, event controls, calls to other tasks) and returns values through output or ref arguments. In classes, time-consuming methods such as driving a bus must be tasks.
explain what a given digital circuit doe: Name the circuit first by its structure: trace the inputs through the gates or flops, write the Boolean equations or the next-state equations, and recognise the function (for example an adder, a mux, a counter or an edge detector). Then write the Verilog in the clearest style: assign statements for combinational logic and an always_ff block for registers, with the same reset behaviour as the circuit, and verify with a small testbench.
how do you write rtl that is efficient i: Performance: pipeline long paths, balance stages, avoid deep priority logic, use one-hot FSMs, and register outputs. Power: gate clocks with enables, avoid unnecessary toggling (operand isolation, hold data when not valid), and reduce memory accesses. Area: share resources such as adders and multipliers across cycles, avoid redundant logic and over-wide signals, prefer RAMs over flop arrays, and keep reset only where needed. Every choice trades one against another.
how would you build a digital clock in v: Divide the board clock (for example 50 MHz) with a counter to make a 1 Hz enable; cascade counters for seconds (0 to 59), minutes (0 to 59) and hours (0 to 23), each incrementing when the previous rolls over; convert each digit to BCD and then to seven-segment codes, and multiplex the displays with a faster refresh enable (around 1 kHz). Add debounced buttons to set the time, use clock enables instead of generated clocks, and constrain the main clock.
walk through the rtl to gdsii flow: RTL (verified) is synthesised with timing constraints into a gate-level netlist, scan and DFT are inserted, and equivalence is checked. In physical design: floorplan (die size, macros, IO, power grid), placement and optimisation, clock tree synthesis, routing and post-route optimisation. Then extraction of parasitics and sign-off: STA across corners, IR drop and EM, crosstalk, DRC, LVS, antenna and density checks, with ECOs to fix issues, and finally the GDSII file is streamed out for tape-out.
draw the bode plot of an op amp s gain v: An internally compensated op-amp has a very high DC gain (100 dB or more) that stays flat up to a low dominant pole (often a few Hz to tens of Hz), then falls at -20 dB per decade, crossing 0 dB at the unity-gain bandwidth (the gain-bandwidth product, for example 1 MHz). The phase drops to -90 degrees after the dominant pole; a second pole near or beyond unity gain sets the phase margin. Closed-loop gain G gives a bandwidth of about GBW / G.
explain how a cmos inverter works: A PMOS connects the output to VDD and an NMOS connects it to ground, with both gates on the input. Input low: the PMOS is on and the NMOS off, so the output is pulled to VDD. Input high: the NMOS is on and the PMOS off, so the output goes to 0. Only during the transition do both conduct briefly. In steady state no current flows, so static power is almost zero and the output swings rail to rail.
explain the operating regions of a cmos: As the input rises: (1) NMOS off, PMOS linear, output high; (2) NMOS saturated, PMOS linear, output starts falling; (3) both saturated around the switching threshold, highest gain; (4) NMOS linear, PMOS saturated; (5) PMOS off, NMOS linear, output low. The steep middle region is where the inverter amplifies and where noise margins are defined.
how do you choose the oscilloscope bandw: The scope's and probe's bandwidth should be about 3 to 5 times the highest frequency of interest so its own response does not distort the signal. For digital signals, the edges matter more than the clock frequency: use the rise time, BW = 0.35 / t_rise (for example a 350 ps edge needs at least 1 GHz, ideally more). Match the probe bandwidth and loading too.
what is a demultiplexer and what is it u: A demultiplexer routes one input to one of several outputs selected by the select lines: with n select bits it has 2^n outputs, and the unselected outputs are 0. It is a decoder with a data input used as the enable. Uses: distributing data to one of several destinations, address decoding (enabling one memory chip or register), and serial-to-parallel conversion.
what is the difference between ram and r: RAM (random access memory) can be read and written during normal operation and is usually volatile, losing its contents without power; it holds working data. ROM (read-only memory) holds fixed contents written at manufacture or programming time and is non-volatile; it holds boot code and firmware. Programmable variants (PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash) blur the line but are still mainly read.
what is the difference between a mutex a: A mutex is a lock with ownership: only the thread that locked it can unlock it, and it protects one critical section. A semaphore is a counter: wait or get decrements it and blocks at zero, signal or put increments it, and any thread can signal; a counting semaphore controls access to N identical resources and can also be used for signalling between threads. A binary semaphore behaves like a mutex without ownership.
what is the difference between the arm w: Both put an Arm core into a low-power standby state. WFI (wait for interrupt) wakes up on an interrupt or a debug event. WFE (wait for event) wakes up on an event, which can be an interrupt but also an SEV (send event) instruction from another core or the event register already being set; it is typically used in spinlocks, so a core waiting for a lock sleeps until the owner signals the release with SEV.
write a program that swaps two values: With a temporary: t = a; a = b; b = t;. Without a temporary, using XOR: a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; (fails if a and b are the same variable or memory location), or with arithmetic: a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b; (can overflow). In Verilog, a non-blocking swap works directly: a <= b; b <= a;.
compare spi and i2c speed clock stretchi: SPI uses four wires (SCLK, MOSI, MISO and one chip select per slave), is full duplex, has no addressing or acknowledgement, and runs at tens of MHz. I2C uses two open-drain wires (SCL, SDA) with pull-ups, has 7- or 10-bit addressing, ACK and NACK, multiple masters with arbitration, and slower speeds (100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz, 3.4 MHz). Clock stretching exists only in I2C: a slave holds SCL low to make the master wait. Test cases: all SPI modes (CPOL and CPHA), chip-select timing, back-to-back transfers; for I2C, address match and mismatch, ACK and NACK, repeated start, clock stretching, arbitration loss, and bus timing at each speed.
how are i2c pull ups configured and how: Each line (SDA and SCL) has one pull-up resistor to VDD, because devices only drive the lines low. The value is a trade-off: small enough that the RC rise time with the bus capacitance meets the spec (for example 1000 ns at 100 kHz, 300 ns at 400 kHz), so Rmax = t_r / (0.8473 Cbus); large enough that a device sinking 3 mA can pull the line below VOL, so Rmin = (VDD - VOL) / IOL. Typical values are 2.2 k to 10 kohm.
explain the setup time of a flip flop: Setup time is the minimum time the D input must be stable before the active clock edge, so the flip-flop can capture it reliably. Internally the master latch needs time for the data to propagate through its input stage before it closes. If data changes inside the setup window, the output may take the wrong value or go metastable. In STA the setup check requires data arrival plus setup time to be no later than the capture clock edge.
how do you verify a multi block ip using: Reuse the block-level environments: each block's agents become passive monitors on internal interfaces, while active agents drive only the IP's external ports. Integrate the block scoreboards and add an end-to-end scoreboard for the full data path, use a virtual sequencer to coordinate traffic across interfaces, use the RAL model for register configuration, and focus the tests on interactions between blocks, shared resources, clocks and resets, and system scenarios, with coverage across blocks.
what is the alternative to an analysis p: Analysis ports broadcast to any number of subscribers through write(). Alternatives: put and get ports (blocking or non-blocking) for point-to-point transfer between two components, a uvm_tlm_fifo or uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo between them to buffer, analysis imps with the `uvm_analysis_imp_decl macro when a component needs several analysis inputs, transport ports for request and response, or, outside TLM, callbacks, events and a shared object handle.
why do we use a virtual sequence what is: A virtual sequence runs on a virtual sequencer that holds handles to several real sequencers, so it can coordinate stimulus across multiple interfaces or agents (for example configure through APB, then start traffic on AXI, then wait for an interrupt). A virtual interface is a handle to a SystemVerilog interface instance, which lets class-based code such as drivers and monitors access the DUT's signals; it is passed in through config_db.
what is the minimum number of gates need: Simplify first: build the truth table or K-map and find the minimal sum of products (or product of sums), then look for shared terms and XOR patterns that reduce the count further, and consider which gate types are allowed (NAND-only or NOR-only designs need converting). Count the gates and literals in the final form, and show that removing any gate changes the function.
debug a piece of systemverilog rtl: Read the code with the spec and look for the usual bugs: blocking assignments in always_ff, missing defaults causing latches, incomplete resets, width mismatches and sign issues, off-by-one counters, wrong FSM transitions, multiple drivers, race conditions and CDC without synchronisers. Simulate with a small testbench to reproduce the failure, trace it in the waveform back to the first wrong signal, then fix it and add an assertion or test so it stays fixed.
what is the pipeline depth of each of se: Count the register stages between each input and the output: every value assigned in an always @(posedge clk) block is one register, so the pipeline depth (latency) is the number of clocked assignments the data passes through. Combinational assigns add no depth. Watch for blocking assignments inside a clocked block, which can collapse what looks like two stages into one, and for feedback that makes the logic sequential rather than a pipeline.
design a mux in cmos: A 2:1 MUX in CMOS can be built with two transmission gates: one passes A when S = 0, the other passes B when S = 1, with an inverter generating S-bar (6 transistors, or 8 with an output buffer). A static complementary version implements y = A S' + B S as an AND-OR-invert followed by an inverter, which restores the level and drives loads better.
design a summing circuit with an op amp: An inverting summing amplifier: each input goes through its own resistor Ri into the inverting input, a feedback resistor Rf goes from the output to the inverting input, and the non-inverting input is grounded. Then Vout = -Rf (V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...). If you swap the inputs (feedback to the non-inverting input), the feedback becomes positive, so the circuit no longer settles at a linear operating point: the output saturates at a rail and behaves like a comparator or latch.
draw a cmos nand gate does its logic cha: Two PMOS in parallel from VDD to the output and two NMOS in series from the output to ground. The logic function does not change with different input delays: in steady state the output is always NAND of the inputs. But the timing does: the delay depends on which input switches (the NMOS nearer the output is faster because the lower node is precharged) and glitches can occur when the inputs change at different times.
draw a cmos inverter and explain how it: PMOS from VDD to the output, NMOS from the output to ground, gates tied to the input. A low input turns the PMOS on (output high); a high input turns the NMOS on (output low). If VDD is removed (floating or 0), the output can no longer be driven high: for a low input it floats or follows leakage, and for a high input the NMOS still pulls it low. The inverter stops working and its inputs may back-power the supply through ESD diodes.
draw a cmos inverter and mark all four t: Each transistor has four terminals: gate, source, drain and body. For the PMOS (pull-up), the source and body connect to VDD, the gate to the input, and the drain to the output. For the NMOS (pull-down), the source and body connect to ground, the gate to the input, and the drain to the output. Tying the bodies this way keeps the junctions reverse biased.
draw a nand gate in cmos and explain how: PMOS A and PMOS B in parallel between VDD and the output; NMOS A and NMOS B in series between the output and ground. When both inputs are 1, both NMOS conduct and both PMOS are off, so the output is 0. If either input is 0, its PMOS pulls the output to 1 and the series NMOS path is open. The pull-down and pull-up networks are duals, so there is never a static path from VDD to ground.
draw an and gate using transistors: A CMOS AND gate is a NAND gate followed by an inverter: two parallel PMOS and two series NMOS make the NAND, then a PMOS and NMOS pair inverts it, 6 transistors in total. There is no single-stage non-inverting CMOS AND gate, because static CMOS stages are naturally inverting.
draw logic gates at transistor level: Inverter: one PMOS to VDD and one NMOS to ground. NAND: parallel PMOS, series NMOS. NOR: series PMOS, parallel NMOS. AND and OR: a NAND or NOR followed by an inverter. XOR: a complementary implementation with 12 transistors, or transmission-gate versions with 6 to 8. General rule: series NMOS for AND, parallel for OR, and the PMOS network is the dual.
draw the cross section of a cmos gate: On a p-type substrate, the NMOS sits directly in the substrate with n+ source and drain diffusions and a p+ body tap to ground; the PMOS sits in an n-well with p+ source and drain diffusions and an n+ well tap to VDD. Both have a thin gate oxide under a polysilicon or metal gate, separated by shallow trench isolation, with contacts up to the metal layers. The well and substrate taps prevent latch-up.
draw the physical cross section of an nm: A p-type substrate (body) with two heavily doped n+ regions (source and drain), a thin gate oxide over the channel region between them, and a polysilicon or metal gate on top, with spacers on the sides. A p+ body contact ties the substrate to ground, and shallow trench isolation separates it from neighbouring devices. When the gate voltage exceeds Vt, an inversion layer of electrons forms the channel between source and drain.
draw the transfer characteristic of an i: Plot Vout against Vin: Vout stays at VDD for low inputs, drops steeply around the switching threshold VM (about VDD/2 for a balanced inverter), and settles at 0 for high inputs. Mark VIL and VIH where the slope is -1, VOH and VOL at the rails, and the noise margins NMH = VOH - VIH and NML = VIL - VOL. A steep transition means high gain and good noise immunity.
explain negative feedback in an op amp: Part of the output is fed back to the inverting input, so the op-amp drives its output in the direction that reduces the difference between its inputs. With very high open-loop gain, the inputs stay at almost the same voltage (the virtual short), and the closed-loop gain is set by the feedback network, for example -Rf/Rin, independent of the op-amp's gain. Negative feedback stabilises the gain and extends bandwidth, lowers distortion and output impedance, at the cost of gain.
find the fanout of a gate from its ioh i: Fan-out is how many inputs one output can drive while staying within logic levels. Compute it for both states: fan-out(low) = IOL / IIL and fan-out(high) = IOH / IIH, and take the smaller of the two. For example IOL = 16 mA, IIL = 1.6 mA gives 10; IOH = 0.4 mA, IIH = 40 uA gives 10, so the fan-out is 10.
find the switching threshold of a cmos n: Treat the gate as an equivalent inverter. With both inputs switching together, the two series PMOS act like one with half the strength (Kp/2 = Kn here) and the two parallel NMOS like one with double strength (2 Kn). Setting the currents equal in saturation: 2 Kn (VM - Vtn)^2 = Kn (VDD - VM - |Vtp|)^2, so VM = (VDD - |Vtp| + sqrt(2) Vtn) / (1 + sqrt(2)), and with Vtn = 2 |Vtp| that becomes VM = (VDD + (2 sqrt(2) - 1) |Vtp|) / (1 + sqrt(2)). If only one input switches, the pull-down is a single NMOS and VM shifts higher.
what is a ring oscillator: A ring oscillator is an odd number of inverters connected in a loop. There is no stable state, so a transition travels around the ring forever, giving a square wave with period 2 N td (N stages of delay td). It is used to measure gate delay and process speed on test chips, as a VCO (with current-starved stages) in PLLs, and as an on-chip clock or random-number source.
what is latch up in cmos: In bulk CMOS, the parasitic PNP (in the n-well) and NPN (in the substrate) bipolar transistors form a PNPN thyristor between VDD and ground. A current injection (from ESD, overshoot, radiation or a supply glitch) can turn both on, each feeding the other, and they latch into a low-resistance path that draws large current until the power is removed, possibly destroying the chip. Prevention: well and substrate taps close together, guard rings around IO, lower well resistance, spacing between NMOS and PMOS, and SOI processes.
what is the switching threshold voltage: The switching threshold VM is the input voltage at which Vout = Vin, the middle of the transfer curve where both transistors are in saturation. Equating their currents gives VM = (Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)) / (1 + r), with r = sqrt(kp / kn). With equal strengths (PMOS about 2 to 3 times wider), VM is about VDD/2; a stronger PMOS raises it and a stronger NMOS lowers it.
which is faster pmos or nmos why: NMOS is faster: electrons have about 2 to 3 times the mobility of holes, so an NMOS of the same size conducts more current and switches a load faster. That is why PMOS transistors are made wider to match, why NAND gates (series NMOS) are preferred over NOR gates (series PMOS), and why pull-down paths are the fast ones.
a 1 uf dram capacitor holds 10 uc and is: The stored voltage is V = Q / C = 10 uC / 1 uF = 10 V. If the cell must not lose more than its whole charge before the refresh after 12.5 ms, the maximum allowed leakage (discharge) current is I = Q / t = 10 uC / 12.5 ms = 0.8 mA; in practice you allow only a fraction of the charge to leak (for example 10% gives 80 uA), so that the sense amplifier still reads the right value.
differences between sram and dram why is: SRAM uses a 6-transistor latch per bit: fast (around 1 ns access), no refresh, made in the standard logic process, but about 4 to 6 times larger per bit. DRAM uses a capacitor and one transistor: dense and cheap, but slower, with destructive reads, refresh, and a special process. Caches need low latency and must sit on the same die as the core, so SRAM is used; DRAM is used for main memory where capacity matters more.
explain c memory layout and the size of: A C program's memory has text (code), read-only data (constants and string literals), initialised data (.data), zero-initialised globals and statics (.bss), the heap (malloc, growing up) and the stack (locals and return addresses, growing down), plus memory-mapped IO in embedded systems. Sizes are platform dependent: char 1 byte, short 2, int usually 4, long 4 or 8, long long 8, float 4, double 8, pointers 4 or 8, and bool (C99 _Bool) usually 1 byte, not 1 bit. Structs add padding for alignment.
explain a complete pipeline stage by sta: Take lw x5, 8(x6) followed by add x7, x5, x8. Fetch: the lw is read from instruction memory at PC. Decode: registers are read (x6) and the immediate 8 is extended; the add follows one cycle behind. Execute: the ALU computes x6 + 8. Memory: the data cache is read at that address. Write-back: the value goes into x5. The add needs x5 in its execute stage, one cycle too early, so the hazard unit inserts one bubble and forwarding passes the loaded value from MEM/WB to the ALU.
explain how a 5 stage pipeline works: Five instructions are in flight at once, each in a different stage: fetch from instruction memory, decode and register read, execute in the ALU, memory access, and write-back to the register file. Pipeline registers between stages hold each instruction's data and control signals. After the pipeline fills, one instruction completes every cycle. Hazards are handled with forwarding paths, a load-use stall, and branch prediction or flushing.
explain pipelining the pipelining parado: Pipelining overlaps instruction execution in stages, raising throughput. Ideal speedup over a non-pipelined design is the number of stages k: n instructions take (k + n - 1) cycles instead of n k. The paradox is that pipelining makes each instruction slower (extra register delay per stage), yet the program runs faster, because more instructions finish per unit time. Real speedup is limited by unbalanced stages, register overhead and hazard stalls: throughput = 1 / (cycle time x CPI).
explain the structure of an soc and a mi: A microprocessor chip is mainly the CPU cores with caches, an interconnect, a memory controller and IO links. An SoC integrates a whole system: CPU clusters, GPU, DSPs and accelerators, memory controllers, on-chip SRAM, a DMA engine, peripherals (UART, SPI, I2C, USB, PCIe), security and boot blocks, clocks, reset and power management, all connected by an on-chip bus or network (AMBA AXI, AHB, APB or a NoC).
how does a gpu pipeline work including t: The driver writes command buffers into memory; the command streamer (front end) fetches and parses them, sets state and dispatches work. In a graphics pipeline, vertices are fetched and processed by vertex shaders, assembled into primitives, clipped and rasterised into fragments, the fragments are shaded by pixel shaders and textured, then depth and stencil tests and blending write the result to the framebuffer. Compute work is dispatched as thread groups across the shader cores (SIMT warps), with caches and memory controllers feeding them.
how many 8 kb chips do you need for a 25: 256 KB / 8 KB = 32 chips. Each 8 KB chip needs 13 address lines (2^13 = 8192), and the full 256 KB needs 18 address lines; the top 5 lines go to a 5-to-32 decoder that selects one chip.
is sram volatile or non volatile and why: SRAM is volatile: each bit is held by the feedback of two cross-coupled inverters, which needs power to keep running. When power is removed, the latch loses its state, and at power-up it settles to a random value. Unlike DRAM it needs no refresh while powered.
what are the performance trade offs betw: Larger caches lower the miss rate but raise hit latency, area and power. Higher associativity reduces conflict misses but costs hit time and energy. Larger lines exploit spatial locality but waste bandwidth and raise miss penalty. Write-back saves bandwidth versus write-through but adds complexity. Inclusive hierarchies simplify coherence but waste capacity; exclusive ones maximise capacity. Multi-level hierarchies balance fast small L1s with large L2s and L3s.
what is a watchdog timer: A watchdog timer is a hardware counter that resets or interrupts the system if software fails to refresh (kick) it within a timeout. Normal software periodically restarts the timer; if the code hangs, crashes or loops, the timer expires and the watchdog resets the chip, recovering from faults without human intervention. Windowed watchdogs also flag refreshes that come too early.
write pipelined code for the fetch and d: Fetch: on each clock, PC <= next_pc; the instruction memory output and PC + 4 go into the IF/ID register (flushed on a taken branch, held on a stall). Decode: split the instruction into opcode, rs, rt, rd and immediate fields, read the register file, sign-extend the immediate, generate the control signals, and write them all into the ID/EX register. The hazard unit compares ID's source registers with a load in EX and stalls (holding PC and IF/ID and zeroing the ID/EX control) when needed.
how is the scan def generated: After scan insertion, the DFT tool writes a scan DEF file that describes the scan chains: each chain's start and stop points, the ordered list of scan flops, and which segments may be reordered (floating or ordered sections, partitions). The place-and-route tool reads it to reorder the chains based on placement, shortening scan wires, and then writes an updated chain order that ATPG must use.
what is the purpose of a lockup latch in: A lockup latch is inserted between scan flops in different clock domains (or with skewed clocks, or opposite edges) on a scan chain. It holds the data for half a cycle, so a late-clocked receiving flop does not capture the new value already shifted out of the earlier flop, avoiding hold violations during shift. It is a level-sensitive latch transparent on the opposite phase of the launching clock.
a 20 w and a 60 w bulb are in series acr: The 20 W bulb. Rated at 120 V, R = V^2 / P gives 720 ohm for the 20 W bulb and 240 ohm for the 60 W bulb. In series they carry the same current, I = 120 / 960 = 0.125 A, so the power is I^2 R: 11.25 W in the 20 W bulb and 3.75 W in the 60 W bulb. The higher-resistance bulb gets more power and glows brighter.
add two numbers without using the operat: Use XOR for the sum without carries and AND for the carries: while (b != 0) { c = (a & b) << 1; a = a ^ b; b = c; } return a;. Other options: a - (-b), or incrementing in a loop, but the bitwise version is what interviewers expect because it mirrors a hardware adder.
can a single port be clocked by multiple: Yes, a port can be launched or captured by several clocks (for example in different modes, or a port feeding flops in two domains). Specify a delay relative to each clock with set_input_delay or set_output_delay using the -clock option, and -add_delay for the second and later ones so they do not overwrite the first, optionally with -clock_fall. Then use set_false_path or clock groups between clocks that can never interact.
explain short circuit current: Short-circuit (crowbar) current flows while a CMOS gate switches: during the input transition, when the input is between Vtn and VDD - |Vtp|, both the PMOS and the NMOS are on, giving a direct path from VDD to ground. It is larger with slow input slews and with fast outputs, and adds about 10 to 20% to dynamic power. Keeping input transitions sharp and balancing input and output slews reduces it.
explain the mosfet regions of operation: Cut-off (VGS < Vt): ID is about 0 (only subthreshold leakage, exponential in VGS). Linear or triode (VDS < VGS - Vt): ID = k [(VGS - Vt) VDS - VDS^2 / 2], a voltage-controlled resistor for small VDS. Saturation (VDS >= VGS - Vt): ID = (k/2)(VGS - Vt)^2 (1 + lambda VDS). Here k = mu Cox W/L. Short-channel devices show velocity saturation, making ID closer to linear in VGS.
explain your current role and responsibi: Describe your scope in one breath: the blocks or subsystems you verify, the methodology (UVM, formal, emulation), and your ownership (test plan, testbench architecture, VIP, coverage closure, regressions, sign-off). Then give one concrete example: the hardest bug you found, how you found it and its impact, plus numbers (coverage, bugs, tape-outs). Mention how you work with designers and architects.
for a 1000 um net how do you compute its: Get the per-unit-length resistance and capacitance for the layer from the technology file or the extraction tables: R per um = sheet resistance / width (plus via resistance), C per um = area, fringe and coupling capacitance for that layer, width and spacing. Multiply by 1000 um: for example 0.1 ohm/um gives 100 ohm and 0.2 fF/um gives 200 fF. Model the wire as a distributed RC (several pi segments) and its Elmore delay is about 0.5 R C plus the driver resistance times the total capacitance.
how do you analyze clock tree reports: Check the summary first: the number of sinks, maximum insertion delay (latency), global and local skew against targets, transition and capacitance violations, and the number and type of clock buffers. Then look at the worst skew pairs and the longest and shortest paths, clock gating cells, crossings between clock domains that need balancing, and the clock tree's power. Compare pre- and post-route numbers and make sure timing uses the propagated clock.
how do you connect components when sever: Use one analysis imp per transaction type, declared with `uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_a) and `uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_b), so the receiver has separate write_a() and write_b() methods. Alternatively use one analysis FIFO per stream and get from each in its own thread, or a common base transaction class with $cast to the specific type in a single write().
how do you detect endianness: Store a multi-byte value and inspect its first byte: uint32_t x = 1; little_endian = (*(uint8_t *)&x == 1);. A union of an integer and a byte array works the same way. Most compilers also provide macros (such as __BYTE_ORDER__), and many CPUs have a status bit showing the configured endianness.
how do you reduce standby leakage power: Power-gate idle blocks (header or footer switches, with isolation and retention for state), use high-Vt cells on non-critical paths, lower the supply in standby (retention voltage for SRAMs), use reverse body bias, stop clocks and put memories into sleep modes, and choose longer channel lengths where speed is not needed. At system level, shut down whole domains in deep sleep.
in design compiler how do you constrain: Clocks: create_clock -period with -name on the clock port, plus set_clock_uncertainty, set_clock_latency and set_clock_transition; create_generated_clock for divided clocks. Inputs and outputs: set_input_delay and set_output_delay relative to the clock, set_driving_cell (or set_drive) on inputs and set_load on outputs. Design rules: set_max_capacitance and set_max_transition on the design or ports (and set_max_fanout). Add exceptions with set_false_path and set_multicycle_path.
reduce p y p y: (P + Y)(P' + Y) = P P' + P Y + P' Y + Y Y = 0 + Y (P + P') + Y = Y. By the distributive law it is directly Y + P P' = Y.
what are the high and low noise margins: Noise margins measure how much noise a logic level can tolerate. NMH = VOH(min) - VIH(min): how far a high output can drop and still be read as high. NML = VIL(max) - VOL(max): how far a low output can rise and still be read as low. VIL and VIH are where the transfer curve's slope is -1. Larger margins mean better immunity to supply noise, crosstalk and ground bounce.
what are the pros and cons of low vt and: Low-Vt cells switch faster (more drive current) but leak much more, exponentially more as Vt drops. High-Vt cells leak far less but are slower. Designs use multi-Vt optimisation: high-Vt (or standard-Vt) cells everywhere by default to save leakage, and low-Vt only on critical paths that need the speed, swapping cells after timing analysis.
what checks are done at each stage of th: RTL: lint, CDC and RDC, functional verification and coverage. Synthesis: timing, area and power reports, design rule violations, equivalence (RTL versus netlist), and DFT DRC. Floorplan and placement: congestion, utilisation, timing and power grid. CTS: skew, latency and transitions. Routing: DRC, opens and shorts, timing, signal integrity. Sign-off: STA in all corners and modes, IR drop and EM, DRC, LVS, antenna, density, equivalence on the final netlist, and gate-level simulation.
what do noise reports and glitch reports: Noise (signal integrity) reports show crosstalk effects: delta delay (aggressors switching in the same or opposite direction speed up or slow down the victim, affecting setup and hold) and functional noise. Glitch reports show bumps induced on a quiet victim net by coupling from switching aggressors: the glitch height and width compared with the receiving cell's noise immunity, because a large enough glitch can flip a latch or flop. Fixes: spacing, shielding, upsizing victims and downsizing aggressors.
what does the volatile keyword do: volatile tells the compiler that a variable may change outside the normal program flow (a hardware register, an ISR or another thread), so every read and write in the code must really access memory: the compiler cannot cache it in a register, remove repeated reads, or reorder those accesses. It does not make accesses atomic or add memory barriers.
what happens if the body is not tied to: If the source rises above the body (for an NMOS, VSB > 0), the body effect increases the threshold voltage, making the transistor weaker and slower, as in stacked transistors. If the body is at a higher voltage than the source (forward body bias for NMOS), the threshold drops, making it faster but leakier; if it exceeds about 0.6 V, the source-body junction becomes forward biased and conducts, which can trigger latch-up. That is why bodies are normally tied to ground (NMOS) and VDD (PMOS).
what is a linker script: A linker script tells the linker how to place the program in the target's memory: it defines the memory regions (flash, RAM with their addresses and sizes), maps the output sections (.text, .rodata, .data, .bss, stack and heap, interrupt vectors) to those regions, sets the entry point, and defines symbols (such as the start and end of .bss) that the startup code uses to copy and clear data. It is essential for embedded and bare-metal code.
what is a multicycle path: A multicycle path is a path that is allowed more than one clock cycle to propagate, because the design only samples its result every N cycles (for example data that is enabled every other cycle). You tell STA with set_multicycle_path N -setup, and usually set_multicycle_path N-1 -hold so the hold check moves back accordingly. The design must guarantee the multicycle behaviour, which should be verified.
what is one hot encoding: One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, with exactly one bit high at a time. Next-state and output logic become simple (often one gate per bit), decoding is fast, and it suits FPGAs with plenty of flops. It uses more flip-flops than binary encoding (N versus log2 N), and needs care to recover from illegal states.
what is the snr of a 16 bit adc: For an ideal N-bit ADC with a full-scale sine input, SNR = 6.02 N + 1.76 dB. For 16 bits that is 6.02 x 16 + 1.76 = about 98.1 dB. Real converters are lower because of noise and distortion, which the effective number of bits (ENOB) captures.
what is the difference between risc and: RISC uses a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions that each take about one cycle, a load-store architecture, many registers and a hardwired control unit, which makes pipelining easy. CISC uses many complex, variable-length instructions with memory operands and multi-cycle execution, often microcoded, for denser code. Modern CISC chips translate instructions into RISC-like micro-ops, so the practical difference is mainly in decode complexity.
what is the difference between a structu: In a struct each member has its own storage, so the size is at least the sum of its members (plus padding for alignment), and all members are valid at once. In a union all members share the same storage, so the size is that of the largest member and only one member is meaningful at a time. Unions are used to save memory or to view the same bits as different types, such as for endianness checks.
what is the difference between modeling: Modelling builds a description that predicts behaviour, such as a SPICE model of a transistor, a timing model of a cell, or an architecture model of a CPU. Characterisation measures or simulates a real circuit across conditions to extract the numbers that go into a model, for example running SPICE on each standard cell across PVT corners, loads and slews to fill the Liberty timing and power tables. Characterisation feeds the models.
what is the difference between sequentia: A combinational circuit's outputs depend only on its present inputs; it has no memory or clock (gates, multiplexers, adders, decoders). A sequential circuit's outputs depend on the present inputs and the stored state, kept in latches or flip-flops, usually updated by a clock (registers, counters, FSMs). Sequential circuits are combinational logic plus memory and feedback.
what is the difference in instruction ex: A RISC CPU fetches fixed-length instructions that are simple to decode, does arithmetic only on registers, and moves data with separate load and store instructions, so each instruction flows through a simple pipeline in about one cycle. A CISC CPU decodes variable-length instructions that may read memory, compute and write memory in one instruction, traditionally taking many cycles through microcode; modern CISC cores split them into micro-ops that execute like RISC instructions.
what is the trade off between dynamic po: Dynamic power falls with lower voltage and fewer transitions, but lower voltage makes transistors slower, which tempts designers to lower the threshold voltage, and leakage rises exponentially as Vt drops. So reducing dynamic power through voltage scaling increases leakage, and fast low-Vt cells increase leakage too. The balance is set per design with multi-Vt cells, DVFS and power gating: low Vt on critical paths, high Vt elsewhere, and gating to remove leakage when idle.
where and when do you use decoupling cap: Decap cells are on-chip capacitors between VDD and VSS placed in the standard cell rows. They supply local charge during sudden current demands, reducing dynamic IR drop and supply noise. Place them near high-activity logic (clock buffers, wide buses, register banks), near power-hungry macros and in empty space after placement. They cost area and add some leakage, so use them where dynamic IR analysis shows hotspots.
which addressing mode does mov ax cx use: It is register indirect addressing: the operand's memory address is held in a register, and AX is loaded from the memory location that the register points to. Note that on the real 8086, only BX, BP, SI and DI can be used as address registers, so MOV AX, [CX] is not a valid 8086 instruction; MOV AX, [BX] is the valid form.
write a sequence item for the input inte: Turn each interface signal that carries information into a field: rand fields for the values you drive (address, data, operation type, length, delays between items), constraints for legal combinations and the scenario's distributions, and non-rand fields for responses the driver fills in. Register it with the factory and field macros or do_copy and do_compare, and add a convert2string for debug. Keep timing out of the item: the driver handles the handshake.
explain the top level pin placement flow: Top-level pin placement assigns each IO or block pin to a location on the die or block edge. It is decided by the package and board (bump and ball map, signal grouping), the location of the blocks that connect to each pin (to shorten routes and meet timing), signal type (high-speed pairs and clocks need special placement and shielding), power and ESD needs, and routing congestion. The flow: get the pin list and constraints, place the pins (often guided by a first trial placement), check timing and congestion, then iterate with block owners.
given block netlists timing constraints: Read the netlists, libraries (.lib), LEFs and constraints, and check them (missing cells, constraint sanity). Set the die and core size from area and target utilisation, define rows and the IO or pin placement, then place the macros: near their related logic and IO, along edges, oriented to keep pins facing the core, with halos and channels for routing. Build the power grid (rings, straps, macro connections), add blockages and endcap and tap cells, then run a quick placement and timing and congestion checks to refine it.
write binary search in pseudocode and gi: lo = 0, hi = n - 1; while lo <= hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if a[mid] == key return mid; else if a[mid] < key then lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid - 1; return not found. The array must be sorted. Time complexity is O(log n) because the range halves each step; space is O(1) for the iterative version.
write merge sort in c and give its time: void merge_sort(int *a, int *tmp, int lo, int hi) { if (hi - lo < 1) return; int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; merge_sort(a, tmp, lo, mid); merge_sort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi); int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo; while (i <= mid && j <= hi) tmp[k++] = (a[i] <= a[j]) ? a[i++] : a[j++]; while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++]; while (j <= hi) tmp[k++] = a[j++]; for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) a[k] = tmp[k]; }. Time O(n log n) in every case; space O(n) for the temporary array; it is stable.
explain the ahb protocol: AHB (AMBA High-performance Bus) is a pipelined bus: each transfer has an address phase and a data phase, and the address of the next transfer overlaps with the data of the current one. Key signals: HADDR, HTRANS (IDLE, BUSY, NONSEQ, SEQ), HWRITE, HSIZE, HBURST (single, incrementing and wrapping bursts of 4, 8 and 16), HWDATA and HRDATA, HREADY for wait states and HRESP for errors. A decoder selects the slave, and in multi-master systems an arbiter grants the bus. AHB-Lite is the single-master version.
what is the difference between axi and a: AXI has five independent channels: write address (AW), write data (W), write response (B), read address (AR) and read data (R), each with its own valid and ready handshake. This allows reads and writes at the same time, multiple outstanding transactions, out-of-order completion using IDs, and burst transfers described only by the start address and length. AHB has one shared address and data pipeline, one outstanding transfer per master, in-order responses and separate arbitration, so AXI gives much higher throughput and better latency hiding.
how do you set inter clock uncertainty: Use set_clock_uncertainty with -from and -to clocks: set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.1 -from [get_clocks clkA] -to [get_clocks clkB], and a separate -hold value. It models jitter and skew between two related clocks (synchronous but from different sources or PLL outputs), and overrides the single-clock uncertainty for paths between those clocks.
complete missing code in a uvm testbench: Go through the testbench in order: check that every component is registered with `uvm_component_utils and created with type_id::create (not new) in build_phase, that super.build_phase is called, the virtual interface is fetched from config_db with the right path and type, the driver and sequencer are connected in connect_phase, objections are raised and dropped around the sequence, and analysis ports are connected to the scoreboard. Then demonstrate a factory override in the test: set_type_override_by_type(base_seq::get_type(), err_seq::get_type()) before the environment is built.
explain uvm callbacks mailboxes and sema: UVM callbacks let users add behaviour to a component without modifying it: the component calls `uvm_do_callbacks at hook points, and a test registers a callback object (for example to inject errors in a driver). A mailbox is a FIFO for passing objects between threads, with put and get (blocking), try_put and try_get, and an optional size bound. A semaphore controls access to a shared resource with get(n) and put(n) of keys, so only one thread (or n) uses it at a time.
explain the systemverilog testbench inte: An interface bundles related signals (and can contain tasks, assertions and modports) so the DUT and testbench connect through one port. A clocking block inside it defines when signals are sampled and driven relative to a clock (with input and output skews), which avoids races between testbench and design. A program block runs testbench code in the reactive region, also to avoid races (less used with UVM). A virtual interface is a handle to an interface instance that class-based code (drivers, monitors) uses to reach the signals.
how do you write an assertion in a uvm t: Concurrent SVA assertions are best placed in the interface (or a checker module bound to the DUT with bind), not in UVM classes, because classes cannot contain concurrent assertions. Write a property on the interface clock with disable iff (reset), assert it with a label and an else $error or `uvm_error message, and add cover properties. Immediate assertions can be used inside classes (for example in the scoreboard or on randomize()). Control them from the test with $assertoff and $asserton or a config knob.
how does a uvm test start: The top module calls run_test(), either with a test name or with +UVM_TESTNAME on the command line. The UVM root uses the factory to create the test as uvm_test_top, then runs the phases on the whole hierarchy: build (the test builds the environment), connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, then run_phase where the test raises an objection, starts its sequences and drops the objection; when all objections are dropped, the extract, check, report and final phases run and the simulation ends.
how would you formally verify a cache: Write properties for the cache's correctness and let the tool prove them for all input sequences: data integrity (a read returns the value of the last write to that address), using a symbolic or chosen address and data with a small reference model to keep the state space small; tag and valid consistency; no two ways holding the same tag; correct dirty-bit and write-back behaviour; coherence-protocol invariants (only one Modified copy) and deadlock or liveness properties for the controller. Use abstractions such as reduced sets, ways and data width, and assumptions on the bus protocol.
what are the uvm phases and why do we us: UVM phases are the ordered steps every component goes through: build (create sub-components top-down), connect (connect TLM ports), end_of_elaboration and start_of_simulation (final checks and printing), run (the time-consuming test, optionally split into reset, configure, main and shutdown), then extract, check, report and final. They are used so that all components are created before they are connected and connected before they run, without any manual synchronisation, and so that results are collected consistently at the end.
what is a deep copy versus a shallow cop: A shallow copy (b = new a;) creates a new object and copies a's properties, but any handles inside it are copied as handles, so both objects point to the same sub-objects; changing a nested object through one copy affects the other. A deep copy also creates new copies of every nested object, so the two are fully independent. SystemVerilog only provides the shallow copy built in; a deep copy needs a custom copy() method (in UVM, do_copy) that calls copy on each nested object.
what is a virtual interface and why is i: A virtual interface is a variable that holds a handle to an interface instance. Classes cannot contain interfaces or ports directly because they are dynamic objects, so drivers and monitors use a virtual interface to access the DUT's signals. The top module instantiates the interface and passes it down (in UVM through uvm_config_db), which keeps the class code reusable with any instance of that interface.
what is the uvm sequencer used for: The sequencer is the arbiter between sequences and the driver. Sequences generate items and send them to the sequencer with start_item and finish_item; the sequencer arbitrates when several sequences run at once (FIFO, priority, random or user-defined), hands items to the driver through get_next_item, and routes responses back to the right sequence. It also supports locking and grabbing for exclusive access and virtual sequencers for coordination.
what is the difference between simulatio: Simulation runs the RTL in software with full visibility, easy debugging and 4-state values, but it is slow (around 10 to 1000 Hz for a large SoC). Emulation maps the design onto special hardware (Palladium, ZeBu, Veloce) and runs at around 1 MHz, fast enough to boot an OS and run software, with less but still good visibility. Formal verification does not run cycles at all: it mathematically proves properties for all possible inputs, exhaustive but limited to smaller blocks.
what is the difference between tasks and: In UVM, as in SystemVerilog, functions execute in zero simulation time and cannot block, so the build, connect, extract, check and report phases are functions (build_phase, connect_phase); tasks can consume time, so run_phase and the run-time sub-phases (reset_phase, main_phase), sequence body() and driver code are tasks. You cannot call a task from a function, so time-consuming work must stay in task phases.
what is the difference between virtual m: A virtual method can be overridden by a derived class, and calls through a base handle run the derived version at run time (polymorphism). A virtual class is an abstract class: it cannot be instantiated with new, only extended, and it can declare pure virtual methods that every concrete derived class must implement. A virtual class can contain both regular and virtual methods.
when building timing constraints do you: Yes, in practice every input and output should be constrained relative to a clock with set_input_delay and set_output_delay (plus drive and load), otherwise those paths are unconstrained and never checked. Exceptions: asynchronous inputs such as an asynchronous reset or signals crossing from other domains, which are synchronised and can be false paths or set_max_delay; static configuration pins (case analysis or false path); and analog or test-only ports. Tools report unconstrained ports, which should be reviewed.
explain how you would write verilog for: Define the states with localparam or a SystemVerilog enum, and use two (or three) always blocks: a clocked block that updates the state register with reset, a combinational block that computes the next state with a case on the current state and a default assignment (to avoid latches), and the output logic, either from the state (Moore) or from state and inputs (Mealy), registered if the outputs must be glitch-free. Include a default for illegal states and choose an encoding (binary, one-hot) that suits the target.
how did you boot your processor in veril: Explain your own design. A typical answer: on reset the PC is set to a fixed reset vector (often 0) in the fetch stage's register; the instruction memory is a ROM or array initialised from a hex file with $readmemh in simulation (or a memory initialisation file on FPGA), and the testbench releases reset after the memory is loaded. The first fetch reads address 0, which holds the start of the program or a jump to it.
how do verilog case statements synthesiz: A case statement in combinational logic becomes a multiplexer selected by the case expression, or a decoder driving the outputs. If the items are mutually exclusive (a full, parallel case), it maps to a parallel mux; overlapping items or casez wildcards give priority logic like an if-else chain. Missing items without a default in combinational logic create latches. In a clocked block, the case logic feeds the flip-flops' D inputs.
what is the difference between functions: A function returns a value, executes in zero simulation time and cannot contain delays or event controls; a task can contain timing controls and consume time, has output arguments instead of a return value, and can call both tasks and functions. A function cannot call a task because the task might consume time, which would break the guarantee that a function completes in zero time (functions are used in expressions and continuous assignments).
write verilog for a 4 bit register: module reg4 (input wire clk, input wire rst_n, input wire en, input wire [3:0] d, output reg [3:0] q); always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if (!rst_n) q <= 4'b0000; else if (en) q <= d; end endmodule. It uses non-blocking assignments, an asynchronous active-low reset and a load enable.
what are multicycle paths and false path: A false path is a path that can never propagate in a real operation (asynchronous crossings with synchronisers, mutually exclusive mux paths, test-only logic): STA should ignore it with set_false_path. A multicycle path is a valid path that is only required to settle in N cycles because the design samples it every N cycles: set_multicycle_path N -setup and N-1 -hold. Both must be justified by the design (and verified, for example with CDC or formal checks), because wrong exceptions hide real violations.
what timing optimization strategies do y: Pre-layout (synthesis): correct and realistic constraints, logic restructuring, retiming and pipelining, resizing and Vt selection, buffering high-fan-out nets, path groups and physical-aware synthesis. Post-layout: placement optimisation (moving and clustering critical cells), gate sizing and Vt swaps, buffer insertion and removal, useful skew in CTS, layer promotion and non-default rules for critical nets, fixing crosstalk with spacing and shielding, and ECOs, while fixing hold with delay cells after setup is met.
how do you optimize power at each stage: Synthesis: clock gating, multi-Vt selection, operand isolation and power-aware mapping. Floorplan: power domains, power switches, macro placement to shorten high-activity wires. Placement: cluster high-activity cells, reduce wire capacitance, use high-Vt cells on non-critical paths. CTS: fewer, well-sized clock buffers and gating close to sinks, since the clock is a large share of dynamic power. Routing and sign-off: reduce wire capacitance, swap leakage-heavy cells to high Vt with timing slack, and verify IR drop and power with real activity.
what process technology challenges affec: Advanced nodes bring tighter design rules and multi-patterning constraints (coloring, cut rules), higher wire and via resistance making routing and IR drop harder, more variation (OCV, local variation, aging, self-heating), FinFET discrete widths, stronger crosstalk, EM limits, more corners and modes to close, density and DFM rules, and pin-access problems in dense standard cells. All of these increase runtime and need more margin.
design asynchronous and synchronous fifo: Synchronous FIFO: a dual-port RAM (or register array), read and write pointers on one clock, and a count or an extra pointer bit to generate full and empty. Asynchronous FIFO: the RAM is written in the write clock domain and read in the read domain; each side keeps binary pointers with one extra bit, converts them to Gray code, and synchronises the Gray pointer into the other domain through two flops. Full is computed on the write side (Gray write pointer equals the synchronised read pointer with the top two bits inverted), empty on the read side (pointers equal); flags are pessimistic but safe.
which rtl coding styles give the best ba: Fully synchronous design with one clock edge, registered outputs and inputs at block boundaries, no latches unless intended, no combinational loops, one clock and reset strategy (synchronous de-assertion), clock gating only through library ICG cells, limited logic depth between registers, avoiding very wide muxes and long priority chains, resource sharing where timing allows, parameterised and readable code, and clean CDC boundaries. These make synthesis, timing closure and DFT smoother.
explain pin density and cell density iss: Pin density is the number of cell pins per area; when too many pins sit in a small region, the router cannot reach them all, causing congestion, detours, DRC violations and timing degradation. Cell density (utilisation) that is too high in an area leaves no room for buffering and routing. Hotspots are these local congestion or high-density regions, often near macros or around highly connected logic. Fixes include cell padding, placement density limits, partial blockages, spreading logic, and using cells with better pin access.
explain the eco methodology: An ECO (engineering change order) applies a small change to a design late in the flow without redoing everything. Functional ECO: the RTL is fixed, then a tool or engineer derives the minimal netlist change (adding, removing or reconnecting a few gates), which is implemented in the placed and routed database using spare cells or new cells, and verified with equivalence checking. Timing ECOs resize cells and insert buffers. After tape-out, metal-only ECOs use pre-placed spare cells so only metal masks change.
how do you set variables in tcl: With set: set name value (for example set period 2.5). Read it with $name; set x [expr {$a + 1}] evaluates an expression; lists with set l {a b c} or [list ...]; arrays with set arr(key) value; global variables with global inside procs. Use unset to delete a variable and info exists to test for one.
how is ir drop analysis done and what st: Static IR analysis uses average power per instance (from switching activity) and computes the voltage drop across the power grid resistance; dynamic IR analysis uses time-based current waveforms (vectorless or from simulation activity) to find peak drops when many cells switch together. Reports give the worst drop per net (VDD and VSS), drop maps showing hotspots, per-instance effective voltage, resistance per path, and electromigration current density violations. Fixes include more straps, vias and decaps, and spreading high-activity cells.
if too many logic cell pins sit in one p: Pin congestion: too many pins to connect in a small area, so the router cannot access them all, causing detours, shorts and opens, DRC violations, longer wires with worse timing and crosstalk. Fix it with cell padding or spreading (placement density screens, partial blockages), using cells with better pin access, avoiding very high-fan-in cells clustered together, reshaping or relocating the logic, and adjusting the floorplan (macro placement, channels).
what is the command for setting a multic: set_multicycle_path N -setup -from <start> -to <end>, usually with set_multicycle_path N-1 -hold for the same paths so the hold check moves back to the original edge. Use -start or -end to choose which clock's cycles are counted when the launch and capture clocks differ.
how do you relate the routing grid to th: The manufacturing grid is the minimum resolution of all layout coordinates (for example 0.005 um); every shape, pin and track must sit on it. The routing grid (tracks) is defined per layer by a pitch and an offset in the technology LEF; the pitch must be a multiple of the manufacturing grid and should match the cells' pin positions so pins are on or reachable from tracks. Check it by comparing the LEF pitches and offsets with the cell rows and pin locations, running a track and pin-access check, and making sure routed wires produce no off-grid DRC errors.
what kinds of routing issues have you fa: Typical ones: congestion around macros and in dense logic, pin-access problems in high-density cells, shorts and opens left after detail routing, DRC violations (spacing, minimum area, via enclosure, end-of-line rules), antenna violations on long nets, crosstalk on long parallel nets, timing degradation from detours, and clock nets needing non-default rules and shielding. Describe one you fixed, for example adding channels or blockages, cell padding, or layer assignment.
define a hash and an array in perl: In Perl, an array is an ordered list indexed by integers, declared with @ (my @arr = (1, 2, 3); $arr[0]). A hash is an unordered set of key-value pairs indexed by strings, declared with % (my %h = (clk => 100, rst => 0); $h{clk}). Arrays keep order and are accessed by position; hashes give fast lookup by name.
what challenges have you faced in place: Pick one real example per area and tell it as a short story. Place and route: congestion near macros or a hold-versus-setup conflict fixed with floorplan changes. Formal: a proof not converging, solved with abstraction or tighter assumptions, or a vacuous proof caught with covers. ECO: a late functional fix done with spare cells and verified with equivalence. Give the problem, your analysis, the fix and the result.
what is the intrinsic gain of a common s: A common-source stage with a current-source load has intrinsic gain gm ro (the maximum, typically 10 to 50 in modern nodes). With source degeneration Rs, the effective transconductance becomes gm / (1 + gm Rs), so the gain falls (about Rd / Rs for large gm Rs) but becomes more linear and predictable. A simple differential pair with a current-mirror load has a differential gain of gm (ro2 || ro4), about half the intrinsic gain. All of them roll off with frequency because of the output pole 1/(Rout CL), and the Miller effect at the input reduces bandwidth further.
draw a cmos inverter and explain everyth: Cover structure (PMOS pull-up, NMOS pull-down, gates tied), operation (one transistor on at a time), the transfer curve and its five regions, the switching threshold and how sizing sets it, noise margins, delay (charging the load capacitance, rise and fall times, effect of sizing and load), power (dynamic C V^2 f, short-circuit during transitions, leakage), and layout (n-well, contacts, the stick diagram). Mention why it is the reference cell for characterising a technology.
what happens if you swap the pmos and nm: With the NMOS in the pull-up and the PMOS in the pull-down, each transistor passes the logic level it is bad at: the NMOS can only pull the output up to VDD - Vtn, and the PMOS can only pull it down to |Vtp|. The circuit no longer inverts (it behaves as a degraded buffer through source followers), output levels and noise margins degrade, and the next stages may draw static current.
what is punch through in cmos: Punch-through happens in short-channel MOSFETs when the drain depletion region extends far enough to merge with the source depletion region. The gate then loses control of the channel, and a large current flows from drain to source even with the transistor off, similar to breakdown. It is prevented with halo or pocket implants, higher channel doping and shallow junctions, and limits how short the channel can be for a given voltage.
design the power supply management for a: Each downstream port needs a power switch with current limiting (500 mA for USB 2.0, 900 mA for USB 3.x, more with USB-PD), over-current detection reported to the hub controller (which disables the port and notifies the host), and a bulk capacitor (at least 120 uF per port per the USB spec) to hold VBUS steady on hot plug, with inrush limiting. The hub itself is either bus-powered (limited to 100 mA per downstream port) or self-powered from an external supply, with a regulator for the hub chip and ESD protection on the data lines.
how do you make a gate s transitions fas: Increase the drive strength (upsize the driving gate, use lower-Vt cells), reduce the load (fewer fan-outs, shorter wires, smaller receivers), insert a buffer to split a large load, raise the supply voltage, and keep the input slew sharp. In layout, reduce wire resistance and coupling, for example with wider wires, higher metal layers and more spacing.
