how would you verify an image processing: Build a reference model of the algorithm (often in C or Python, called through DPI) that takes the same input image and produces the corrected output, and compare outputs pixel by pixel in the scoreboard. Stimulus: real images and synthetic ones with defective pixels in every position (corners, edges, adjacent defects, defects in each colour channel, frame boundaries), random noise, all-black and saturated frames, and different resolutions and back-pressure. Coverage on defect position and pattern types, and assertions on the video interface timing.
what is the difference between tasks and: Functions execute in zero simulation time, cannot contain delays or event controls, return a value (or are void) and can only call other functions. Tasks can contain timing controls and consume time, return results through output arguments, and can call tasks and functions. Use functions for calculations and tasks for timed operations such as driving a bus.
which part of a hardware design holds bi: State is held in sequential elements: flip-flops and latches (registers, counters, FSM states) and memories (SRAM, register files, ROM) store the bits. Inside a flip-flop or SRAM cell, the bit is kept by cross-coupled inverters (feedback); in DRAM it is the charge on a capacitor. Combinational logic holds no information: it only computes from the stored bits and the inputs.
how would you verify a verilog design: Write a verification plan from the spec listing features and checks, then build a self-checking testbench: drive directed tests for the basic functions and constrained-random tests for the rest, check outputs automatically against a reference model or scoreboard, add assertions for protocol and invariants, measure functional and code coverage, and run regressions until coverage closes. Lint and CDC checks, and formal for critical blocks, complete the picture.
write code to verify a cache: Keep a reference memory model (an associative array) in the testbench and route every access through both the cache and the model: on each read compare the cache's data with the model, on each write update the model. Drive random reads and writes over a small address range to force hits, misses, conflicts, evictions and write-backs, check that dirty lines are written back with the right data, add assertions on the memory-side protocol, and collect coverage on hit and miss per set and way, evictions, dirty write-backs and back-to-back hazards.
solve a transmission gate circuit proble: A transmission gate is an NMOS and a PMOS in parallel with complementary gate signals, so it passes both 0 and 1 without threshold loss when enabled and is high impedance when disabled. To solve a circuit, find for each control combination which gates conduct, trace the input values through the conducting paths to the output, and check for floating outputs (no path conducts) or contention (two conducting paths with different values). Common circuits: a 2:1 MUX, an XOR and a latch.
when do you need to partition a system a: When the design does not fit in one FPGA: too many LUTs, flip-flops, block RAMs or DSPs, too many IO pins, or a design too large to meet timing in one device. This is typical for ASIC prototyping of large SoCs. Partitioning then needs care with signals crossing between FPGAs (limited pins, so time-multiplexing or high-speed links), clock distribution across boards, and timing across the partitions.
explain the cmos inverter and its charac: The CMOS inverter is a PMOS pull-up and an NMOS pull-down with their gates joined. Characteristics: rail-to-rail output, almost no static power, a sharp voltage transfer curve with a switching threshold set by the PMOS-to-NMOS ratio, good noise margins, propagation delay proportional to the load capacitance and inversely to drive current, dynamic power C V^2 f plus short-circuit and leakage power, and very high input impedance (capacitive load).
what does a dma controller do: A DMA (direct memory access) controller moves data between memory and peripherals, or between memory regions, without the CPU copying every word. The CPU programs source and destination addresses, length and mode (and descriptor chains for scatter-gather), starts the transfer and is free for other work; the DMA performs bus transactions and raises an interrupt when done. It saves CPU time and power and gives higher throughput for bulk transfers.
build a mealy fsm using d flip flops: Draw the Mealy state diagram, make the state table with next state and output for each state and input, assign binary codes to the states, then write the D input of each flip-flop as the next-state bit (D = Q next) and simplify with K-maps; the output equations depend on both the state bits and the inputs. Implement the D equations and output equations with gates feeding the flip-flops, and add a reset.
describe a typical test environment moni: A typical environment has a generator or sequence producing stimulus, a driver converting transactions to pin activity, a monitor observing the pins and rebuilding transactions, a scoreboard comparing observed results with a reference model, functional coverage collectors, assertions on the interfaces, an agent bundling the driver, monitor and sequencer per interface, an environment holding the agents and scoreboard, and the test configuring and starting everything, with the DUT connected through interfaces.
explain rc integrator and differentiator: An RC integrator is a series resistor with the output taken across a capacitor to ground: when the time constant RC is much longer than the input's period, the output approximates the integral of the input (a square wave becomes a triangle); it is also a low-pass filter. An RC differentiator has the capacitor in series and the output across the resistor: when RC is much shorter than the period, the output approximates the derivative (a square wave becomes spikes at each edge); it is also a high-pass filter. Op-amp versions give precise integration and differentiation.
explain the asic flow: Spec and architecture, RTL design, verification, lint and CDC, synthesis with SDC constraints, DFT insertion and equivalence checks, then floorplan, placement, CTS and routing with timing optimisation, then sign-off: STA in all corners and modes, power and IR drop, signal integrity, DRC, LVS and antenna checks, and finally tape-out of GDSII, fabrication and silicon testing.
explain the serdes architecture: A SerDes converts parallel data to a high-speed serial stream and back. Transmit: encoding (8b/10b, 64b/66b or 128b/130b) and scrambling, a serializer clocked by a high-speed PLL, pre-emphasis or FFE equalisation, and a current-mode or voltage-mode driver. Receive: termination, CTLE and DFE equalisation to undo channel loss, clock and data recovery (CDR) to extract the clock from the data, a deserializer, alignment and decoding. Modern links use PAM4 and ADC-based receivers with DSP.
what are luts in an fpga: A LUT (look-up table) is the basic logic element of an FPGA: a small memory with k inputs (typically 4 to 6) that stores the 2^k output bits of a truth table, so it can implement any k-input Boolean function; the inputs act as the address. LUTs are configured by the bitstream and are combined with flip-flops, carry chains and multiplexers in logic blocks. Some LUTs can also be used as small RAMs or shift registers.
what are start and stop bits: In asynchronous serial (UART), the line idles high. A start bit (a 0) marks the beginning of a frame, so the receiver can synchronise its sampling to the falling edge, then the data bits follow (usually LSB first, 5 to 9 bits) with an optional parity bit, and one or two stop bits (1) return the line to idle and give time before the next frame. They let the receiver frame each character without a shared clock.
what are the design guidelines for a hig: Control impedance (50 ohm single-ended, 100 ohm differential) with a proper stackup and continuous reference planes under every high-speed trace; keep differential pairs tightly coupled and length matched; minimise vias and stubs (back-drill), and avoid crossing plane splits; keep traces short and spaced to reduce crosstalk; terminate correctly; give good power integrity with low-inductance decoupling close to pins and plane capacitance; and simulate signal and power integrity before fabrication.
what is the asic design flow: The ASIC design flow goes from specification and architecture to RTL coding and verification, then synthesis to gates with constraints, DFT insertion and equivalence checking, then physical design (floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing), then sign-off (STA, power, IR drop, DRC, LVS), tape-out, fabrication, packaging and testing.
why is isolation needed in a upf power i: When a power domain is switched off, its outputs float or go to unknown values, which can cause wrong logic and crowbar current in the always-on domains that receive them. Isolation cells clamp those signals to a known value (0, 1 or the last value) while the domain is off, enabled by an isolation signal from the power controller. Retention keeps register state during shutdown using retention flops with a separate always-on supply and save and restore signals. In UPF: set_isolation with -clamp_value, -isolation_signal and location; set_retention with save and restore signals; and a power controller sequence (isolate, save, power off; power on, restore, release isolation).
draw the stick diagram of a cmos inverte: Draw two horizontal rails (VDD at the top, ground at the bottom), a p-diffusion strip in the n-well near VDD and an n-diffusion strip near ground, and a vertical polysilicon line crossing both to form the gates (the input). Connect the PMOS source to VDD and the NMOS source to ground with contacts, and join both drains with a metal line as the output. Mark the n-well and the colour code (green diffusion, red poly, blue metal).
which input files does the physical desi: The gate-level netlist (Verilog), timing constraints (SDC), the technology LEF (layers, rules, vias) and cell and macro LEFs (abstracts), timing libraries (.lib) for all corners, RC extraction data (QRC or tech files, capacitance tables), power intent (UPF), and the IO or pad and bump information, plus optionally a floorplan DEF and scan DEF. Sign-off adds the GDS libraries and DRC and LVS rule decks.
how do you debug a timing violation in t: Confirm it is timing: the failure should depend on frequency, voltage and temperature. Run a shmoo (frequency against voltage) to find the failing region, then lower the frequency or raise the voltage to see if it passes. Localise it with scan at-speed tests and diagnosis, or with internal debug (failing patterns pointing to specific flops), then correlate with STA paths near that logic, considering IR drop, crosstalk and on-chip variation. Confirm by changing clocks or adjusting delays (for example with tunable delay cells) and fix with an ECO or a frequency limit.
explain uvm sequencer driver communicati: The sequence calls start_item(item), which waits for the sequencer to grant it; it then randomizes the item and calls finish_item(item), which hands it to the sequencer. The driver, connected through seq_item_port to the sequencer's seq_item_export, calls get_next_item(req), receives that item, drives it on the interface and calls item_done() (optionally with a response), which unblocks finish_item in the sequence. Responses can also be returned with put_response and collected with get_response.
how is a systemverilog interface made an: Declare it with interface my_if (input logic clk); logic valid, ready; logic [31:0] data; ... endinterface, optionally with modports for each side (master and slave directions), a clocking block for testbench timing, and tasks or assertions. Instantiate it in the top module, connect it to the DUT ports (or pass it as a port), and give it to the testbench as a virtual interface. It bundles related signals, removes repetitive port lists, and keeps protocols in one place.
write code for a uvm driver a sequencer: Item: class txn extends uvm_sequence_item with rand fields. Sequencer: typedef uvm_sequencer #(txn) my_sequencer; (usually no extra code). Driver: class my_driver extends uvm_driver #(txn); with a virtual interface fetched in build_phase and a run_phase loop: seq_item_port.get_next_item(req); drive it; seq_item_port.item_done();. Agent connect_phase: drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export);. For other TLM: the monitor declares uvm_analysis_port #(txn) ap; created in build_phase, written with ap.write(t), and connected in the environment to the scoreboard's analysis_export or imp.
debug given verilog code and find its er: Read the code with a checklist: syntax and declaration errors, blocking versus non-blocking misuse, incomplete sensitivity lists, missing defaults causing latches, reset bugs, width mismatches and truncation, wrong signed arithmetic, multiple drivers, combinational loops, off-by-one counters and wrong FSM transitions. Then compile, run lint, simulate with a directed testbench to see where outputs first diverge, and fix one bug at a time.
how do you break a combinational loop: A combinational loop is logic that feeds back to itself without a register. Break it by inserting a flip-flop (or latch, if level-sensitive behaviour is intended) in the feedback path, or by restructuring the logic so the output does not depend on itself, for example by computing the next value from registered state. In RTL it usually comes from a signal assigned in terms of itself in an always @(*) block, or from two blocks feeding each other; lint and synthesis tools report them.
how do you generate a ramp signal in ver: Use a counter that increments by a step every clock (or every N clocks) and wraps or saturates at the maximum: always @(posedge clk) if (rst) ramp <= 0; else ramp <= ramp + STEP;. A sawtooth wraps naturally at 2^N; a triangle reverses direction at the limits. The counter value drives a DAC or a waveform viewer as an analog-looking ramp; in a testbench you can also use a real variable with a delay loop.
how does an always block run if it has n: An always block with no sensitivity list and no timing control (always begin a = b; end) runs forever in zero time: it loops again immediately, so simulation time never advances and the simulator hangs. Every always block needs a sensitivity list (@(...)) or a delay or event control inside, for example always #5 clk = ~clk; for a clock generator.
in which situations does synthesis repor: Synthesis errors come from unsynthesizable or illegal constructs: multiple drivers on the same signal from different always blocks, mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments to the same variable, using delays, initial blocks or system tasks in design code where not supported, loops with non-constant bounds, unsupported data types (real), missing or unresolvable modules, and port width or connection errors. Latches, combinational loops and incomplete sensitivity lists usually give warnings rather than errors.
what happens to an oscillating circuit i: A combinational loop with an odd number of inversions (like a ring oscillator in RTL) has no stable state. In simulation it oscillates in zero time or with the given delays: with zero delays the simulator iterates forever in one time step and hangs or hits an iteration limit. Synthesis does not model oscillation; it warns about a combinational loop and builds the gates anyway, and static timing breaks the loop arbitrarily. Real oscillators should be designed as custom or library cells.
what is casex used for in verilog: casex treats X and Z values in the case expression or the items as don't care, so items can use x as wildcards (for example 4'b1xxx matches any value with the MSB 1). It is used for priority decoding. Its risk is that X values from uninitialised signals also match, hiding bugs in simulation; casez (only Z and ? are wildcards) or SystemVerilog case inside are safer.
where are lint tools used can they debug: Lint tools check RTL early, before simulation and synthesis, for coding problems: unintended latches, width mismatches, multiple drivers, combinational loops, incomplete sensitivity lists, clock and reset misuse, unused signals, naming and style rules, and synthesis and simulation mismatch risks. They report syntax errors because they parse the code, but they do not debug functional behaviour; they find structural issues statically.
write a state machine in verilog: Use a typed state: typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, RUN, DONE} state_t; state_t st, nx;. Register: always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) st <= IDLE; else st <= nx;. Next state: always_comb begin nx = st; case (st) IDLE: if (start) nx = RUN; RUN: if (finish) nx = DONE; DONE: nx = IDLE; default: nx = IDLE; endcase end. Outputs: assign busy = (st == RUN); (Moore) or from state and inputs (Mealy).
describe the flow for implementing a chi: In Innovus: read the netlist, LEFs, libraries (through an MMMC view file with corners and constraints) and UPF; floorplan (die size, rows, IO and pin placement, macros, halos), power planning (rings, stripes, rails); placement with place_opt_design; pre-CTS optimisation; clock tree synthesis with ccopt_design and post-CTS optimisation including hold; routing with routeDesign or route_opt_design and post-route optimisation; then add fillers, check DRC and connectivity, extract RC, run timing analysis, and write out the DEF, netlist and GDS for sign-off.
what is the difference between true and: A true dependency (RAW, read after write) is real data flow: an instruction needs the value produced by an earlier one, so it must wait or be forwarded. False dependencies come from reusing register names, not from data flow: WAR (write after read, an anti-dependency) and WAW (write after write, an output dependency). Register renaming removes false dependencies by giving each write a new physical register.
draw a notch filter: A notch (band-stop) filter rejects a narrow band around a frequency f0 and passes the rest. The classic passive form is the twin-T network: a T of two resistors R with a capacitor 2C to ground, in parallel with a T of two capacitors C with a resistor R/2 to ground, giving f0 = 1/(2 pi R C). Active versions add an op-amp buffer with feedback to sharpen the Q. An LC series resonator shunted to ground is another simple notch. It is used to remove mains hum or interference.
write the memcpy function: void *my_memcpy(void *dst, const void *src, size_t n) { unsigned char *d = dst; const unsigned char *s = src; while (n--) *d++ = *s++; return dst; }. It copies byte by byte; behaviour is undefined if the regions overlap (use memmove then). Optimised versions copy word-sized chunks after aligning the pointers, and handle the leftover bytes at the ends.
an op amp draws 20 a into its positive s: Kirchhoff's current law: the currents into the op-amp must sum to zero. 20 A flows in at the positive supply pin and 14 A flows out at the output (input bias currents are negligible), so 20 - 14 = 6 A must flow out of the negative supply pin.
design an op amp circuit with a gain of: A non-inverting amplifier with gain 1 + Rf/Rg: choose Rf = Rg (for example 10 kohm each) for a gain of exactly 2, with the input on the non-inverting pin, Rf from the output to the inverting pin and Rg from the inverting pin to ground. For an inverting gain of -2, use Rf = 2 Rin with the input through Rin to the inverting pin.
draw a cmos inverter and explain how it: A PMOS from VDD to the output and an NMOS from the output to ground, with both gates on the input. A low input turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off, pulling the output up to VDD; a high input turns the NMOS on and the PMOS off, pulling it to ground. Only one network conducts in steady state, so no static current flows, and the output swings fully between the rails.
draw a non inverting op amp and write it: Input to the non-inverting (+) terminal, a feedback resistor Rf from the output to the inverting (-) terminal, and Rg from the inverting terminal to ground. Gain = Vout / Vin = 1 + Rf / Rg. It is always at least 1, the input impedance is very high, and Rf = 0 (with Rg open) gives a unity-gain buffer (voltage follower).
draw an inverter s voltage transfer curv: Plot Vout against Vin from 0 to VDD. Region 1: NMOS off, PMOS linear, Vout = VDD. Region 2: NMOS in saturation, PMOS linear, Vout starts to drop. Region 3: both in saturation at the switching threshold VM, the steepest part with high gain. Region 4: NMOS linear, PMOS saturated. Region 5: PMOS off, NMOS linear, Vout = 0. Mark VIL and VIH where the slope is -1 to define the noise margins.
draw an inverting op amp amplifier and d: Input through Rin to the inverting (-) terminal, Rf from the output to the inverting terminal, and the non-inverting terminal grounded. The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the current through Rin, Vin / Rin, all flows through Rf (the op-amp input draws no current): Vin / Rin = -Vout / Rf, so the gain is Vout / Vin = -Rf / Rin.
draw an inverting op amp and derive its: With the non-inverting input grounded, negative feedback holds the inverting input at virtual ground. The current Vin / Rin flows through Rf, so Vout = -(Rf / Rin) Vin. The output is inverted and scaled by the resistor ratio, and the input impedance is Rin.
draw the pmos and nmos transistors separ: Each MOSFET has four terminals: gate, source, drain and body. The NMOS symbol has the arrow on the source or body pointing inward (or out from the channel on the source), the PMOS has the arrow pointing outward and often a bubble on the gate. In circuits, the NMOS source and body usually go to ground and the PMOS source and body to VDD; current flows from drain to source in an NMOS and from source to drain in a PMOS.
draw the cross section of a transistor a: NMOS cross-section: p-type substrate, n+ source and drain, thin gate oxide and a gate above the channel, with a p+ body contact. The body effect: when the source is at a higher potential than the body (VSB > 0), the depletion region under the gate widens, more charge is needed to invert the channel, and the threshold voltage rises: Vt = Vt0 + gamma (sqrt(2 phiF + VSB) - sqrt(2 phiF)). It weakens stacked transistors and source followers.
explain cmos technology and its advantag: CMOS uses complementary NMOS and PMOS networks, so in steady state there is no path from supply to ground: static power is almost zero. Compared with bipolar, NMOS-only or TTL logic, CMOS gives much lower power, full rail-to-rail swing and high noise margins, very high input impedance and fan-out, high density, and it scales well with process shrinks, which is why almost all digital ICs use it. Its costs are speed per gate versus bipolar (historically), leakage in advanced nodes and latch-up.
explain a cmos concept you know for exam: Pick one and explain it fully. For example the CMOS inverter: structure, the transfer curve, the switching threshold set by sizing, noise margins, and delay. Its gate capacitance is the input load seen by the driving gate: roughly Cox W L plus overlap capacitances for both transistors, varying with the operating region; the Miller effect makes the gate-drain capacitance appear larger during switching. This capacitance sets the delay of the previous stage and the dynamic power C V^2 f.
how does an inverter s delay change when: The delay grows roughly linearly with load capacitance: t_d is about 0.69 Reff (Cload + Cpar), where Reff is the equivalent resistance of the driving transistor and Cpar its own drain capacitance. Doubling the load roughly doubles the load-dependent part of the delay and slows the output slew, which slows the next stage too. Upsizing the inverter lowers Reff but increases its input capacitance.
what is breakdown voltage draw the v i c: The breakdown voltage is the reverse voltage at which a diode suddenly conducts large current, through avalanche multiplication or Zener tunnelling. The V-I curve: in forward bias, almost no current until about 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon, then the current rises exponentially; in reverse bias only a tiny leakage current flows until the breakdown voltage, where the current rises sharply at a nearly constant voltage (which Zener diodes use for regulation).
what is the output voltage of an inverti: For an ideal inverting amplifier, Vout = -(Rf / Rin) Vin. For several inputs in a summing configuration, Vout = -Rf (V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...). The output is limited by the supply rails, so it saturates if the ideal result exceeds them.
what limits an op amp s bandwidth: The gain-bandwidth product, set by the dominant-pole compensation that keeps it stable, which makes the gain fall at -20 dB per decade, so closed-loop bandwidth is about GBW divided by the closed-loop gain. For large signals the slew rate also limits the bandwidth (full-power bandwidth = SR / (2 pi Vpeak)). Load capacitance and the second pole reduce phase margin, which in practice limits usable bandwidth too.
why does a virtual short appear between: With negative feedback and a very large open-loop gain A, the output Vout = A (V+ - V-) stays finite, so the input difference must be tiny (Vout / A, microvolts). The inputs therefore sit at almost the same voltage, which is the virtual short, while no current flows into them because of the high input impedance. If the non-inverting input is grounded, the inverting input is a virtual ground.
how do sram reads and writes behave when: Larger pass-gate (access transistor) resistance makes reads more stable but slower: the cell discharges the bit line more slowly, so the read takes longer, but the storage node is disturbed less (a better read static noise margin). Writes become harder: the bit-line driver has to overpower the cell's pull-up through a weaker path, so writes slow down and can fail at low voltage. SRAM sizing balances the pull-down, pass-gate and pull-up ratios for both.
how would you verify the interface betwe: Build agents on the CPU side (as a master issuing reads and writes) and on the memory side (as a responder model), with a reference memory in the scoreboard. Test single and burst reads and writes, byte enables and alignment, back-to-back and outstanding transactions, address boundaries, wait states and back-pressure, error responses for invalid addresses, reset during transfers, and ordering rules. Add protocol assertions on the interface and coverage on transaction types, sizes and addresses.
what is the voltage after charge sharing: Charge is conserved on the node(s) that are connected when the switch closes. Write the total charge before (sum of C_i V_i for capacitors referenced to the same node), then after connection all connected capacitors share one voltage: V_final = sum(C_i V_i) / sum(C_i). For capacitors stacked in series, the same charge flows through each, so the voltage splits in inverse proportion to capacitance. Energy is lost in the switch resistance.
why does a dma controller have multiple: Multiple channels let several independent transfers be set up at once (for example audio, UART, SPI and memory copies), each with its own source, destination, length, priority and trigger. They share the bus, so an arbiter interleaves their transfers in time (round-robin or priority) at burst granularity; with multiple bus ports or a crossbar, some can run truly in parallel. Peripheral request lines start the matching channel, and each raises its own interrupt when done.
a zener rated for 10 ma is in series wit: It depends on the Zener voltage Vz, which the question needs. If Vz is below 10 V, the Zener regulates and the current is I = (10 - Vz) / 1 kohm, for example 4.9 mA for a 5.1 V Zener, well within the 10 mA rating (the maximum, 10 mA, would only happen with Vz = 0). If Vz is above 10 V, the Zener never breaks down and almost no current flows.
compare the power of an and gate driven: Dynamic power is the sum over nodes of alpha C V^2 f. With 400 MHz and 200 MHz clocks on the two inputs (aligned, 50% duty), the inputs toggle at 400 and 200 MHz, and the output is high only when both are high, giving a 200 MHz pulse train with 25% duty, so the output switches at 200 MHz. With both inputs tied to one clock, the output simply follows that clock: at 400 MHz the output switches twice as often (plus both inputs at 400 MHz); at 200 MHz all nodes switch at 200 MHz. Compare by adding the switching rate of each node times its capacitance.
design a calculator from logic gates: Define the operations (for example add, subtract, multiply on small numbers), then build the datapath: an adder-subtractor (adder with XOR on one input and carry-in for subtraction), a multiplier (array or shift-and-add), a mux selecting the result by the operation code, registers for the operands and result, a keypad encoder for input and BCD conversion with seven-segment decoders for output, and a small FSM controlling entry, operation and display.
design a circuit that turns a 2 v input: That is a gain of -5, so use an inverting amplifier with Rf / Rin = 5, for example Rin = 10 kohm and Rf = 50 kohm: Vout = -(50k / 10k) x 2 V = -10 V. The op-amp needs a negative supply beyond -10 V (for example plus and minus 15 V), or a rail-to-rail part with enough headroom.
design a flip flop from nand gates then: Build an SR latch from two cross-coupled NAND gates, add two NAND gates gated by the clock to make a gated D latch, then connect two latches in master-slave form with opposite clock phases to get an edge-triggered D flip-flop (or use the classic 6-NAND edge-triggered design). Counters: chain T or D flip-flops with Q-bar fed back to D so each toggles; connect each flop's output to the next flop's clock for a ripple counter, or clock them all together with AND logic for enables in a synchronous counter.
design a simple low pass filter then tur: Low-pass: a series resistor R and a capacitor C to ground, with the output across C: fc = 1/(2 pi R C), passing low frequencies and rolling off at -20 dB per decade above fc. Swap the positions to make a high-pass filter: the capacitor in series and the resistor to ground, with the output across R, blocking DC and passing frequencies above the same fc.
draw a differentiator: Passive: a capacitor in series with the input and a resistor to ground, with the output across the resistor; it approximates the derivative when RC is much smaller than the signal period. Active: an op-amp with the capacitor C in series with the inverting input and a resistor R in feedback, non-inverting input grounded: Vout = -R C dVin/dt. In practice add a small series resistor with C and a capacitor across R to limit high-frequency gain and noise.
explain sdf back annotation and the spef: After place and route, parasitic extraction writes the wire resistances and capacitances to a SPEF file. The STA tool reads the netlist, libraries and SPEF, computes cell and net delays, and checks timing. It can write the computed delays to an SDF file, which gate-level simulation back-annotates onto the netlist to simulate with real delays. Correlation means checking that delays from different tools agree: for example, the place-and-route tool's internal timing against sign-off STA with sign-off extraction, adjusting margins or settings when they differ.
explain an rc low pass filter: A series resistor and a capacitor to ground, with the output across the capacitor. At low frequencies the capacitor's impedance is high, so the output follows the input; at high frequencies the capacitor shorts the output to ground. The cut-off frequency fc = 1/(2 pi R C) is where the output is -3 dB (0.707 of the input) with a -45 degree phase shift; above it the gain falls at 20 dB per decade. In the time domain, a step input gives an exponential rise with time constant RC.
explain how a mosfet works: A MOSFET has a gate separated from the channel region by a thin oxide. For an NMOS, a gate voltage above the threshold attracts electrons to the surface, forming a conducting channel between the n+ source and drain (inversion). The gate voltage controls the channel's conductivity, so the drain current is controlled by voltage with almost no gate current. With small VDS it acts as a resistor (linear region); with larger VDS the channel pinches off near the drain and the current saturates. A PMOS works the same way with holes and opposite polarities.
explain the timing closure flow methodol: Start with clean, complete constraints and a clean synthesis netlist. Close setup first: fix the worst paths by logic restructuring, sizing, Vt swaps, buffering, useful skew and floorplan or placement changes; at the RTL level, pipeline or retime. After CTS, fix hold with delay cells without breaking setup. After routing, handle crosstalk and the extracted parasitics, and analyse all corners and modes with OCV derates. Iterate with ECOs until every path meets timing in sign-off STA. Common issues: bad constraints, congestion detours, long nets, and setup-hold conflicts.
for an iir filter with a 0 875 how many: For y[n] = x[n] + a y[n-1] with a = 0.875, the output depends directly on only one past output, but recursively on all past inputs, with weights a^k that decay geometrically (that is what infinite impulse response means). In practice, count how many terms matter: 0.875^k drops below 1% after about 35 samples (ln 0.01 / ln 0.875), and below 10% after about 17.
given a digital circuit with a fault whi: Activate the fault and propagate it: set the faulty node to the value opposite its stuck value using the primary inputs, then set the side inputs of every gate on a path from that node to an output to their non-controlling values (1 for AND and NAND, 0 for OR and NOR) so the difference reaches the output. Justify all of these values back to the inputs; the resulting input vector detects the fault in a single pass, since the good and faulty circuits produce different outputs.
given a post route database and function: Get the functional change as an RTL fix and a reference netlist, then use a logic ECO tool (or manual edits) to find the minimal gate changes to the implemented netlist. Implement them in the routed database: use spare cells for metal-only changes or place new cells near the affected logic, then route the changed nets incrementally. Checks: logical equivalence between the new RTL and the ECO netlist, STA for setup, hold and transitions across corners, DRC, LVS and antenna, IR drop if large, and DFT (scan chains still intact).
given one gate s rise time and the load: For the same driver, the rise time is proportional to the load capacitance (t is about 2.2 R C for 10% to 90%), so t2 = t1 x C2 / C1. If the drivers differ, scale by their drive strengths too: t2 = t1 x (R2 C2) / (R1 C1). Include each gate's own output (parasitic) capacitance in C if given.
how can a half bridge rectifier give the: A half-wave rectifier passes only one half of the AC cycle, so its output has gaps and more ripple. To get full-wave rectification with only two diodes, use a centre-tapped transformer: each half of the secondary feeds one diode, so both half cycles produce current through the load in the same direction, giving the same output as a full-bridge (but each half of the winding only supplies the peak of its own half, so the transformer needs twice the secondary voltage).
how do you measure an unknown resistance: Put the ammeter in series with the resistor and the voltmeter in parallel across it, apply a known voltage, and compute R = V / I. For a small resistance, connect the voltmeter directly across the resistor (the ammeter outside it), so the ammeter's resistance does not add to the measurement; for a large resistance, put the ammeter right next to the resistor inside the voltmeter's connection, so the voltmeter's current does not add to the measured current.
how does an oscilloscope work and what i: An oscilloscope displays voltage against time. The input goes through a probe and an attenuator and amplifier, is sampled by a high-speed ADC (in digital scopes), stored in memory and drawn on the screen, with a trigger circuit that starts each capture at a chosen event (an edge or a pattern) so repetitive signals appear stable. It is used to look at waveforms, measure amplitude, frequency, rise time, jitter and timing relationships between signals, and to debug glitches and noise.
name five measurable characteristics of: Frequency (or period), duty cycle, rise and fall times, amplitude and voltage levels (overshoot and undershoot), jitter (period, cycle-to-cycle, phase jitter), phase noise, and skew relative to another clock.
simplify a 5 variable function with a k: Draw two 4-variable K-maps, one for E = 0 and one for E = 1, side by side. Group 1s within each map as usual, and also between the maps: a cell in one map is adjacent to the same cell in the other map. A group that appears in the same position in both maps drops the variable E. Write the minimal sum of products from the largest groups. Quine-McCluskey is the systematic alternative for 5 or more variables.
sketch the output of an rc filter withou: Think in terms of the capacitor's voltage not changing instantly and the time constant tau = RC. For an RC low-pass with a step input, the output rises exponentially toward the input, reaching 63% after one tau and nearly 100% after 5 tau; a square wave gives rounded edges if the period is long compared with tau and a triangle-like wave if it is short. For an RC high-pass, the output jumps with the input edge, then decays exponentially to 0.
what are bjts and mosfets and how do the: A BJT (bipolar junction transistor) is a current-controlled device with an emitter, base and collector: a small base current controls a larger collector current (Ic = beta Ib), with high transconductance and good matching, but it draws base current. A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled device with a gate, source, drain and body: the gate voltage controls a channel, with essentially no DC gate current and very high input impedance. MOSFETs dominate digital and dense ICs; BJTs remain in analog, RF and power niches.
what happens when two capacitors are con: Capacitors in series carry the same charge, so the total capacitance is lower than the smallest one: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 (for two, C = C1 C2 / (C1 + C2)). The applied voltage divides in inverse proportion to capacitance, V1 / V2 = C2 / C1, so the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage. Series connection is used to raise the voltage rating or to make capacitive dividers.
what is the average output voltage of a: The average equals the duty cycle times the voltage applied when the switch is on: for a source V switched across the resistor 40% of the time and 0 otherwise, the average output is 0.4 V (for example 4 V from 10 V). If an RC filter follows, the output settles to that average with some ripple.
what is the difference between combinati: A combinational circuit's output depends only on its current inputs (no memory), like adders and multiplexers. A sequential circuit's output depends on its current inputs and its stored state, held in flip-flops or latches and usually updated by a clock, like counters, registers and state machines.
what is the high frequency content of a: A PWM signal is a square wave at the switching frequency whose average (the low-frequency content) carries the wanted signal. The high-frequency content is the switching frequency and its harmonics (plus sidebands around them from the modulation), which must be filtered out with a low-pass filter (or the load's own inductance) to recover the average. Sharp edges add harmonics far above the switching frequency, which matters for EMI.
why choose a particular feedback resisto: In a feedback network the resistor value sets the gain (for example Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg) or the regulator output voltage, and its absolute value trades current consumption (larger values draw less), noise (larger values add more thermal noise and are more sensitive to input bias currents and leakage) and bandwidth (larger values form slower poles with stray capacitance). If the value changes, the gain or output voltage changes with it; tolerance and temperature coefficient matter for accuracy; and the power rating must cover the dissipation.
what issues have you faced with clock ga: At synthesis, the integrated clock gating cells must be inserted correctly and their enable timing checked (clock gating setup and hold). At placement, gating cells must sit near their flops, or the enable path becomes critical. At CTS, gating cells add clock insertion delay and skew, so the tree must balance gated and ungated sinks, and the enable timing changes once the clock is propagated. After routing, crosstalk on enables and clock nets. Typical fixes: cloning gating cells, moving them closer to the sinks, and constraining the enable paths.
write a program that prints hattrick whe: Scan the string with a counter: for each character, if it is 'w' increment the counter, otherwise reset it to 0; when the counter reaches 3, print 'hattrick' (and decide whether overlapping runs count again). In Python: if 'www' in s: print('hattrick'). In hardware it is a small FSM or a 2-bit counter on the serial character stream.
explain uvm testbench components phases: Components: the test, environment, agents (sequencer, driver, monitor), scoreboard, coverage collectors, and sequences and sequence items, all created through the factory and configured with config_db. Phases order the work: build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, run (with optional reset, configure, main and shutdown sub-phases), extract, check, report and final. TLM ports connect components: the seq_item port between driver and sequencer, analysis ports for one-to-many broadcast from monitors, and put, get and FIFO ports for point-to-point transfers.
how are timing constraints developed: Start from the specification: clocks (sources, frequencies, duty cycle, generated clocks), their relationships (synchronous or asynchronous groups), and the IO timing from the interface specs or the budgets of neighbouring blocks (input and output delays, drive and load). Add clock uncertainty for jitter and skew, then exceptions such as false paths, multicycle paths and case analysis for modes, justified by the design. Validate the constraints with checks (unconstrained paths, clock coverage) and refine them as the design matures.
what is the difference between systemver: SystemVerilog is a language: a hardware description and verification language that extends Verilog with classes, constraints, coverage, assertions and interfaces. UVM is a methodology and class library written in SystemVerilog: it provides a standard structure (components, phases, factory, config_db, TLM, sequences, reporting) for building reusable testbenches. You need SystemVerilog to use UVM, but you can write testbenches in SystemVerilog without UVM.
what synthesis strategies optimize timin: Write tight, correct constraints, then: higher compile effort and incremental optimisation, ungrouping hierarchy so logic can be optimised across boundaries, register retiming, path groups to focus on critical paths, critical-range optimisation, resizing and low-Vt cells on critical paths, buffering and register duplication for high-fan-out nets, and physical-aware (topographical) synthesis for realistic wire delays. At the RTL level, pipeline long paths and restructure deep logic.
